A lung mass (over 3 cm) in a smoker is carcinoma until proven otherwise. Cavitation is seen mainly in squamous cell carcinoma (central necrosis); the wall of a neoplastic cavity is thick and irregular (over 15 mm is highly suspicious), whereas an abscess has a more regular wall, an air-fluid level and an infectious clinical context.
For the T stage, diameter (T2b 4-5 cm, T3 5-7 cm, T4 over 7 cm) and relationships matter: invasion of the visceral pleura leads to T2, of the chest wall to T3; separate nodules in the same lobe T3, in another ipsilateral lobe T4. Broad contact with the pleura is not enough to say invasion: more reliable signs are rib erosion, infiltration of extrapleural fat or muscles, localized pain.
Beware of pseudolesions: in the lowest slices the liver dome, cut obliquely, may look like a round nodule near the heart; it is recognized by scrolling through the images.
